app_title: Didaskalos: Frequency-Based Greek Grammar Textbook Builder
subtitle: An Ancient Greek grammar textbook generated from the texts you choose — lessons ordered by what your corpus actually uses, exercises taken from it unaltered.
intro_html:
Three choices make a book: pick your texts below, and set the lesson count and the textbook type in the sidebar. Press Build Textbook and Didaskalos reads those texts, ranks their grammar by how often each feature occurs, and assembles a book you can download as Markdown or HTML — with the syllabus and token tables as CSV.

Project site  ·  GitHub
how_it_works_html:
What happens when you press build

Nothing is prepared in advance. Every book is computed from the texts you picked, in four stages.

  1. Read. The selected files are downloaded and handed to a per-format adapter — Perseus/AGDT XML, or CoNLL-U for Universal Dependencies and PROIEL. Each adapter rewrites every token's morphology into one shared nine-position tag, so that the two annotation schemes can be counted together; the mapping is close rather than lossless, and where the schemes analyse a form differently it is the normalization that decides. Every token keeps its lemma, its sentence and its citation — the citation as the treebank gives it, over whichever edition that treebank annotates.
  2. Count. Each token is bucketed by the grammatical feature it exhibits — the case of a noun or adjective, the tense–mood–voice triple of a verb, infinitives and participles included, each ranked as its own topic — and those counts become a ranked list. For a declension-based book, nouns and adjectives are first sorted into declension classes, read off the genitive singular and the gender, and the classes are ranked instead of the bare cases.
  3. Order. The ranking is then overruled in four places. Seven starter modules open the book whatever the counts say. Prerequisites declared by kind hold a lesson back until the one it contrasts with has been taught: an irregular class waits for a regular one of the same part of speech, and an adjective class waits for a noun class. A few lessons teach something no paradigm carries and so have no place in the ranking at all; each is set instead against what the reader has already met — deponent verbs (media tantum) after the middle voice, conditional sentences once every mood they are built from has been taught, and an introduction to the Didakta grammar reference once four parts of the nominal system have — and a book too short to reach those forms leaves the lesson out rather than teaching over them. And labels that would only repeat one another are merged, so the vocative is taught inside the nominative. Frequency arranges everything that is left.
  4. Assemble. Each surviving topic pulls in its lesson module, a vocabulary list of the words that most often do that lesson's job in your texts, its exercises, and two rings showing how much of the vocabulary and how many of the forms in your texts the book has covered so far. The book closes with continuous reading passages and a colophon naming every source corpus, its license and its URL.

How the exercises are chosen

Every exercise sentence is a real sentence from your texts — selected, not written. The candidates are the sentences containing the form the lesson teaches, and each is scored on three factors: the mean rarity of its content words (weighted 0.35), the rarity of its single rarest word (0.35), and its length (0.30). Rarity is measured inside your own selection rather than against a general frequency list for Greek, and the scale is rebuilt for each book, so a word that counts as rare in a short selection may be a common word in Greek at large. Sentences in which at least 70 per cent of the content words have already been introduced are offered first, and the rest fill the quota when the corpus cannot supply enough.

Why a build takes a moment

All of this runs on the server, from scratch, every time you press the button: the treebank files are fetched, every token is parsed, the counts are rebuilt, and the whole book is written out. The scale is what makes it slow rather than instant — the Iliad alone comes to 128,102 analyzed tokens and 132 ranked topics. One short work is ready in a few seconds; a large selection across several authors takes considerably longer. The page will keep waiting for it, so give it time rather than reloading.
feedback_html:
Didaskalos is a work in progress, and the lesson modules are being revised all the time. A book you build next week may not be identical to the one you build today — if you need a copy that will not change, keep the file you download. But that shouldn't be the default: it's worth rebuilding from the same texts once in a while to pick up the improvements.

If you use it and find an error anywhere — in a lesson, a paradigm, an exercise or an answer key — I would be very grateful if you reported it to me. Feedback from users is what drives the improvements.

textbook_type_help: Case-based arranges noun/adjective lessons by case (one lesson for accusative, one for genitive, ...). Declension-based first classifies every noun and adjective in the treebanks into declension classes (o-stem, a-stem, etc.) and arranges the lessons by how frequent each class is in the corpus.
custom_treebank_urls_help: One URL per line or comma-separated. These are added on top of the default treebanks loaded from didaskalos/treebanks/perseus.

no_treebanks_warning: No treebanks available. Provide treebank URLs or upload XML files.

results_note: Exercises are unaltered corpus sentences, scored by word rarity and sentence length and preferring sentences whose vocabulary earlier lessons have already introduced, so lexical difficulty climbs without any sentence being reworded; syntactic difficulty is not scored. Download the book as Markdown or HTML (your browser can print the HTML to PDF) and the tables as CSV. Every book carries a colophon naming each source corpus, its license and its URL.
lesson_modules_note: The lesson modules were first drafted by a retrieval pipeline over Smyth's *Greek Grammar* and Crosby & Schaeffer's *An Introduction to Greek*; that pipeline is now [retired](https://github.com/farnoosh-shamsian/didaskalos/tree/main/archive/ragbot). Every module has since been edited, translated and fact-checked with Claude, and I am still hand-correcting them: the review is ongoing rather than finished, so keep this file if you need a copy that will not change. Two things follow. A module I have not yet reached may still carry a small error, and the treebanks are far too large to check by hand, so an occasional annotation slip passes straight into the parsing answers. If you are learning without a teacher, treat anything puzzling as a possible mistake rather than a rule you have not met — and [tell me about it](https://farnoosh-shamsian.github.io/pages/contact.html).

tb_setting_body: This textbook is built for **{lesson_count}** lessons, drawn from **{work_count}** work(s) — or the portions of them that the source treebanks annotate — totalling **{token_count:,}** analyzed word tokens, organized {mode}.

tb_corpus_custom: Custom or uploaded treebank files provided at build time.
tb_corpus_desc_perseus: The Perseus Ancient Greek Dependency Treebank (AGDT), a scholarly collection of syntactically annotated Classical Greek texts maintained by the Perseus Digital Library.
tb_corpus_desc_gorman: Vanessa Gorman's Ancient Greek Dependency Trees, a large set of annotated treebanks covering the Attic orators, historians, and other prose authors.
tb_corpus_desc_harrington: J. Matthew Harrington's treebanked commentaries, published through the Perseids platform.
tb_corpus_desc_proiel-nt: The Greek New Testament from the PROIEL treebank, a morphologically and syntactically annotated edition of the New Testament in Koine Greek.
tb_caveats_body: The parsing answers are derived from the annotation in the source treebanks rather than written by hand, so where a treebank is wrong the answer key is wrong with it. The lesson modules are revised continually and this file is a snapshot: a book built later will not be identical to this one. Exercise sentences are unaltered but excerpted, so one may open with a connective answering a context that is not on the page. And where the texts above span more than one dialect or period, the syllabus is averaged over all of them. Corrections are welcome and gratefully received: [get in touch](https://farnoosh-shamsian.github.io/pages/contact.html).

tb_vocab_prompt: The words that most often do this lesson's job in the texts this book is built from. A few of them belong to another part of speech and are working here as this one; the handful of function words commonest of all are listed once in *Using a Greek Dictionary* rather than repeated. They are given in dictionary form, without translations: look each one up, and write down the meaning you find.
tb_vocab_lookup_hint: The module *Using a Greek Dictionary* explains how to read an entry.
tb_vocab_lookup_cell: Read the entry for {headword} in [Perseus]({perseus_url}), or in [Logeion]({logeion_url}).
tb_core_words_note: This is the last of the fixed opening modules. From here on every exercise sentence is real Greek from your own texts, and these are the words you will meet most often in them. The frequency column shows how often each occurs, and the links give you its dictionary form. They carry very little meaning on their own — they hold a sentence together rather than say what it is about — so look through them now but do not dwell on them. Their precise sense is often hard to pin down in isolation, but it becomes clear with practice, as you meet the words again and again while reading more text. For now, simply aim to recognize them on sight.
